name: Plan discharges and transitions from inpatient medicine and surgical units
function: clinical support: patient flow and discharge planning
summary: From the day a patient is admitted, the care team plans when and how the patient will leave: the physician sets an estimated discharge date, nurses and a patient care coordinator review barriers at daily bullet rounds, and social workers and the home care coordinator arrange home services or a post-acute bed for the minority who need them. When the patient is medically ready the physician writes the order, the nurse teaches the patient and family, and the unit clerk frees the bed. Discharges are slowed by estimated dates that are missing or stale, late home care referrals, fewer physicians and receiving facilities on weekends, and afternoon departures that leave admitted patients waiting in the ED overnight.

baseline.org_archetype: A three-site Ontario community hospital corporation with about 640 beds, hospitalists on medicine, a hybrid electronic and paper chart, and hospital-based home care coordinators.
baseline.notes: Covers medicine, surgical, step-down and complex care discharges. Maternity, paediatric and psychiatric discharges follow shorter routines and are not modelled.

unit_of_work: one inpatient discharge from a medicine, surgical or complex care unit
trigger: A patient is admitted to an inpatient unit and the admitting nurse starts the discharge risk screen.
end_state: The patient has left the hospital with instructions, the bed is released for cleaning, the chart is in health records and the discharge summary is dictated; or the patient is designated ALC and handed to the ALC process.

volume.seasonality: Medicine discharges rise in January to March with respiratory illness; surgical discharges fell during the 2020 and 2021 COVID-19 pauses in scheduled surgery.

evidence.note: Organisation file gives 2,000 to 2,600 inpatient discharges a month for all units. The author removes about 360 obstetric, 100 paediatric and 120 psychiatric discharges a month (births driver 333 to 391 a month and unit sizes in the organisation file).

surge.cause: winter respiratory virus season (influenza, RSV, COVID-19 waves)

evidence.note: Author's estimate of winter medicine admission peaks in Ontario community hospitals.

Nurses screen for complicated discharge on admission, teach the patient and discharge them (oag2010). FTE is the author's estimate of the discharge share of inpatient nursing time on medicine and surgical units; surgical units do the same steps with surg_rn. Loaded costs are the organisation file's ranges: hourly wage x 1.35 (about 25% benefits and HOOPP pension plus 10% overhead). Physician costs are gross clinical earnings paid by the province, not hospital payroll. Roles added here use the same 1.35 factor.
Surgical inpatient nurses do the nursing steps for about a third of discharges; the steps are written for med_rn. Author's estimate.

The physician decides when a patient can leave, writes the discharge order and the discharge summary (oag2010). Surgeons and consultant specialists do the same for their own patients. FTE is the author's estimate.
Unit clerks record expected discharge dates, process the ADT discharge and send the chart to health records. Author's estimate.
Social workers on the multidisciplinary team assess post-discharge needs and arrange placements (oag2010). FTE is the author's estimate.

Most Ontario large community hospitals had nurse discharge planners or patient care coordinators who led bullet rounds and made home care referrals; oag2010 describes the in-charge nurse leading rounds. The organisation file has no such role. Author's estimate of 12 to 15 people at three sites.
Medication reconciliation at discharge is required by Accreditation Canada (oag2010). Pharmacists do it for high-risk patients in many hospitals; FTE is the author's estimate.
Chairs the daily patient flow huddle where delayed discharges are escalated. Author's estimate.

roles.title: Home and community care coordinator based in the hospital (employed by the LHIN / HCCSS)
roles.department: Home and Community Care Support Services (outside the hospital)

evidence.note: The hospital-based CCAC (later LHIN home care, then HCCSS) care coordinator assesses eligibility and arranges home care (oag2010). Employed outside the hospital, so no hospital FTE is stated; their minutes appear in the simulated labour cost.

systems.name: Hospital information system (electronic patient record with ADT, order entry, results, eMAR and clinical documentation)
Electronic bed board and patient flow dashboard
Home and community care referral portal (Health Partner Gateway)
Email, telephone, pagers and wireless phones
Fax (referrals, requisitions and reports to community physicians)
Pharmacy information system and automated dispensing cabinets
Document imaging and scanning of paper chart forms

steps.name: Screen for discharge risk on admission
steps.description: When the patient arrives on the unit, the admitting nurse completes the admission assessment in the electronic record, including the discharge risk screen: who the patient lives with, stairs at home, mobility before admission, current home care and whether the patient can return to the same living situation.

error.defect_description: Living situation or pre-admission function recorded incompletely, so complex needs surface late

evidence.note: oag2010 says a nurse assesses unplanned admissions for risk of a complicated discharge; minutes are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Set the estimated discharge date
steps.description: At the first morning rounds after admission, the hospitalist reviews the working diagnosis and enters an estimated discharge date and the likely destination in the electronic record, using the expected length of stay for the case type as a starting point.

error.defect_description: Estimated date not set or not updated as the patient's course changes

evidence.note: oag2010 says the date should be set on or soon after admission but was often missing or not updated; oag2016 found two of three hospitals did not update expected stays. Minutes are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Post the date on the unit whiteboard and bed board
steps.description: The unit clerk copies the estimated discharge date and destination onto the unit whiteboard and the electronic bed board, and colour-codes the patient as leaving within 24 hours, in two to three days, later, or waiting for another level of care.

error.defect_description: Board not updated, so the bed flow team plans with a stale date

evidence.note: Colour-coded whiteboards on medicine wards are described in oag2010. Minutes are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Review the patient at daily bullet rounds
steps.description: Each weekday morning the patient care coordinator runs a short bullet round with the charge nurse, physiotherapy, social work and, when available, the home care coordinator. Each patient gets about a minute: medical readiness, estimated date and open barriers. Minutes here add up the rounds over the stay.

error.defect_description: Barrier not raised until the day of discharge

next.condition: needs social work, home care or placement planning
expected to go home without new services

evidence.note: Daily bullet rounds on medicine wards, weekly or twice weekly on surgical wards, usually led by in-charge nurses, with physicians and CCAC staff often absent (oag2010). Over 20% of patients need support after discharge (oag2010). The 30% share is the author's estimate.

steps.name: Assess psychosocial needs and options
steps.description: The social worker meets the patient and family, reviews supports at home, finances, caregiver strain and capacity concerns, explains what home care, rehabilitation or other settings can offer, and records the preferred plan in the chart.

evidence.note: The multidisciplinary team including social workers assesses post-discharge needs (oag2010). Social workers work weekday hours. Times are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Collect therapy recommendations
steps.description: The patient care coordinator reads the physiotherapy and occupational therapy assessments in the chart for mobility, equipment and home safety recommendations, and chases any assessment still outstanding with the therapist by phone.

next.condition: family meeting needed to agree the plan

evidence.note: Author's estimate; therapy assessments come from the allied health referral process, which has thin weekend cover.

steps.name: Hold a family meeting
steps.description: The social worker books a meeting with the patient, family or substitute decision-maker, the hospitalist and a therapist, reviews the patient's function and risks, and agrees the destination: home with services, rehabilitation, or a long-term care application.

evidence.note: Author's estimate; waits depend on when family members can attend, often outside weekday hours.

steps.name: Escalate a long-stay barrier at the patient flow huddle
steps.description: For patients heading to long-term care or with no clear destination, the patient flow manager reviews the case at the daily flow huddle with the unit managers, checks the Home First option of going home with extra home care while waiting, and asks the team to prepare the ALC designation.

evidence.note: Author's estimate of common Ontario practice under the Home First approach used in 2019 to 2022.

steps.name: Confirm the destination and start referrals
steps.description: The patient care coordinator records the agreed destination in the chart and on the board and decides which referrals to send: home care through the provincial portal, a rehabilitation or complex care application, or nothing new.

next.condition: home with new home care services
rehabilitation, complex continuing care or convalescent care
long-term care or no available destination
home with family support or outpatient follow-up only

evidence.note: Destinations in 2009: 74% home, 10% home with home care, 4% long-term care, 2% rehabilitation, 2% complex continuing care (oag2010). Shares within the complex group are the author's estimate from these figures.

steps.name: Refer the patient to home care
steps.description: The patient care coordinator completes the home care referral in the Health Partner Gateway, attaches the therapy notes and medication list, gives the expected discharge date and phones the hospital-based home care coordinator.

error.defect_description: Referral sent late or on the discharge day, leaving no time to arrange services

evidence.note: Nurses or social workers contact the CCAC; one in three to two in three referrals missed the agreed notice period, and one CCAC saw 31% same-day referrals (oag2010). Minutes are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Assess eligibility for home care
steps.description: The home care coordinator reviews the referral, sees the patient at the bedside, completes the standard assessment and decides which nursing, personal support or therapy services the patient is eligible for.

evidence.note: CCACs assess eligibility and arrange home care; referrals sent on Fridays or weekends are not answered until the next week (oag2010). Times are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Arrange home care services
steps.description: The home care coordinator contracts nursing and personal support visits with service provider agencies, sets the start date and sends the service confirmation to the unit. If an agency cannot staff the visits, the patient waits in hospital.

next.condition: services not available when the patient is medically ready

evidence.note: About 10% of hospital patients wait for home care, half of them 8 days or less (cihi_homecare, 2017 to 2024 data). In 2009 ALC patients waiting for home care waited six days on average (oag2010).

steps.name: Apply for rehabilitation or complex care
steps.description: The social worker completes the referral form for an inpatient rehabilitation, complex continuing care or convalescent care program, attaches the therapy and medical notes and faxes or uploads it to the receiving program.

evidence.note: The hospital arranges rehabilitation, complex continuing care and palliative placements itself (oag2010). Times are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Receiving program reviews the referral
steps.description: The rehabilitation or complex care program screens the referral, may ask for more information, and either offers a bed date or places the patient on its wait list. Many programs do not admit on weekends.

next.condition: bed offered before the patient is medically ready
no bed yet when the patient is ready

evidence.note: Rehabilitation and complex care facilities accept fewer patients on weekends (oag2010, oag2016). 19% of ALC patients wait for rehabilitation, complex or convalescent care (oag2016). Times and shares are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Confirm medical readiness and write the discharge order
steps.description: When the patient has recovered enough, the physician confirms that discharge criteria are met, writes the discharge order and prescriptions, and reconciles discharge medications against home medications. The wait before this step is the remaining clinical stay, longer on weekends when fewer physicians discharge.

error.defect_description: Medication changes not reconciled with the home list

control.basis: Public Hospitals Act: the physician determines when a patient is discharged, and a discharged patient must leave within 24 hours (as summarised in oag2010)

evidence.note: Physicians decide discharge (oag2010); weekend discharges are about 25% fewer because fewer physicians and staff are on duty (oag2016). Average acute stay 6 days in Ontario 2009/10 (oag2010); stay length is the author's estimate.

steps.name: Designate the patient alternate level of care
steps.description: The physician documents that the patient no longer needs acute care but cannot leave because the destination is not available, and records the designation date and intended destination so the ALC team can take over the case.

control.basis: Provincial ALC definition and Wait Time Information System ALC reporting (Ontario Health)

evidence.note: The discharge destination is set by the physician or delegate with the interprofessional team (alc_method). 5.8% of Canadian hospital stays had ALC days in 2021-2022 (cihi_stays).

steps.name: Reconcile discharge medications
steps.description: A pharmacist compares the discharge prescriptions with the best possible medication history taken on admission, checks doses and stopped drugs, flags discrepancies to the physician and prints a medication list for the patient.

control.basis: Accreditation Canada Required Organizational Practice: medication reconciliation at care transitions

evidence.note: Accreditation Canada requires medication reconciliation; only 10% to 30% of sampled discharge summaries had one in 2009 (oag2010). Times are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Teach the patient and family
steps.description: The nurse reviews the discharge instructions, new medications, warning signs and follow-up appointments with the patient and family, asks them to repeat key points back, and gives the printed instructions.

error.defect_description: Patient leaves unsure about medications or follow-up

evidence.note: Patients receive pamphlets and are told their discharge date and needs (oag2010). Minutes are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Wait for the ride and see the patient off
steps.description: The nurse removes the intravenous line, returns belongings and medications, and waits with the patient for family or transport to arrive. The bed stays occupied until the patient leaves, often in the afternoon.

evidence.note: About 65% of discharges happen between 9 a.m. and 3 p.m. while admissions peak 6 to 8 a.m. (oag2010); discharges drop from 4 p.m. (oag2016). Minutes are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Discharge the patient in the ADT system
steps.description: The unit clerk enters the discharge time and destination in the admission-discharge-transfer module, which frees the bed on the bed board, and phones environmental services if the cleaning request does not go automatically.

error.defect_description: Discharge entered late, so the bed looks occupied and cleaning starts late

evidence.note: 68% of large community hospitals relied on wards to call housekeeping for a bed (oag2016). Minutes are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Post the dirty bed and send the cleaning request
steps.description: The bed board marks the bed as needing cleaning and sends the request to the environmental services queue, where it is worked largely in order of arrival rather than by the type of bed patients are waiting for.

evidence.note: Rooms are cleaned mostly first come, first served (oag2016); fewer than a third of large community hospitals had a hospital-wide bed system, so some sites phone instead.

steps.name: Assemble the chart and send it to health records
steps.description: The unit clerk gathers the paper parts of the chart (consents, flow sheets, outside documents), checks the patient labels, and puts it in the bin collected by health records for scanning and coding.

error.defect_description: Loose sheets missing or filed in the wrong chart

evidence.note: Author's estimate of a hybrid electronic and paper record common in Ontario community hospitals in 2019 to 2022.

steps.name: Dictate the discharge summary
steps.description: The physician dictates or types the discharge summary: diagnosis, treatment, discharge medications with reasons for changes, pending results and follow-up. The summary goes to transcription and then to the family physician.

error.defect_description: Summary late or missing medication changes

control.basis: Medical staff rules on health record completion (suspension of admitting privileges for overdue records)

evidence.note: One hospital required summaries within 10 working days; at others 72% or only 7% were signed within 10 days (oag2010). Times reflect dictation shortly after discharge, the author's estimate for 2019-2022.

exceptions.name: Same-day home care referral
exceptions.description: The need for home care is noticed on the discharge day, the referral goes in late and the patient either leaves without services starting or stays another day.

exceptions.name: Weekend readiness
exceptions.description: The patient becomes medically ready on a Saturday or Sunday but the covering physician is not comfortable discharging, or the receiving facility does not admit on weekends, so discharge waits for Monday.

exceptions.name: Destination not ready
exceptions.description: Home care, a rehabilitation bed or long-term care is not available when the patient is ready, so the physician designates the patient ALC.

benchmarks.unit: days from admission to dictated summary
benchmarks.population: medicine and surgical inpatients in a large Ontario community hospital, excluding ALC days

evidence.note: Author's estimate: median acute stay of about 4 days plus about a day to the dictated summary. Ontario's average stay was 6 days in 2009/10 (oag2010) and the Canadian age-adjusted average 7.2 days in 2021-2022 including ALC days (cihi_stays); averages exceed medians because stays are skewed.

benchmarks.population: acute inpatient stays in Canada, 2021-2022, age-adjusted

benchmarks.unit: share fewer daily discharges on weekends

pain_points.description: Estimated discharge dates are missing or not updated, so bed planning and family preparation start late.

evidence.note: oag2010 found dates often absent or stale; one hospital's whiteboards missed 45% of next-day discharges. oag2016 found two of three hospitals did not update expected stays.

pain_points.description: Home care referrals arrive late, often on the discharge day, and Friday referrals wait until the following week.

evidence.note: Compliance with notice periods was 10% to 54%; one CCAC region had 31% same-day referrals.

pain_points.description: Fewer discharges on weekends and after 4 p.m. leave admitted patients waiting in the ED overnight.

evidence.note: 25% fewer weekend discharges; admitted patients waited 11.6 hours on average overnight.

pain_points.description: Bullet rounds often lack the physician and the home care coordinator, so they settle little beyond whether a patient leaves today.

evidence.note: Physicians attended routinely at one of three hospitals; CCAC staff at one.

assumptions: Nursing and physician steps are written for medicine (med_rn, hospitalist); surgical units run the same steps with surg_rn and the attending surgeon.

The patient care coordinator (RN discharge planner) is not in the organisation file; most Ontario large community hospitals had such a role in 2019-2022. If the hospital had none, the charge nurse and social worker share these steps.
The home care coordinator is employed by the LHIN home care organisation (HCCSS from 2021), not the hospital; their time is in the simulated labour cost but no hospital FTE is stated.
The clinical stay itself is represented by the calendar wait before s15; the steps model only discharge planning work, not treatment.

The simulated median (about 6 days) is above the 5-day benchmark because complex cases add social work, home care and post-acute waits; the stated FTE (46) exceeds the simulated hands-on need (39) because surg_rn time is stated separately while surgical nursing steps are simulated under med_rn.
Deaths in hospital are handled by med-end-of-life-care and are not counted here.
Volume is reduced from the organisation file's 2,000 to 2,600 because obstetric, paediatric and psychiatric discharges are not linked to this process in the organisation file.

Loaded costs are the organisation file's ranges: hourly wage x 1.35 (about 25% benefits and HOOPP pension plus 10% overhead). Physician costs are gross clinical earnings paid by the province, not hospital payroll. Roles added here use the same 1.35 factor.
